1.title: ADM PHASES E & F — PLANNING THE DELIVERY
1.text: Welcome to Module 5. We've defined the architecture across Phases B, C, and D — now we have to plan how to actually deliver it. That's the job of Phases E and F. Phase E, Opportunities and Solutions, identifies how we'll deliver. Phase F, Migration Planning, turns that into a detailed, sequenced plan. This is the bridge between "what" and "how and when" — and the difference between these two phases is one of the exam's very favourite things to test. So let's get it crystal clear.

1.title: Module Overview & Learning Objectives
1.text: Here's our plan for the module. You'll be able to explain the purpose of Phases E and F and exactly how they differ. You'll describe work packages, Transition Architectures, and capability increments. You'll meet two key techniques — the Consolidated Gaps, Solutions and Dependencies matrix, and the Implementation Factor catalog — plus the Business Value Assessment used to prioritize. You'll understand how the Architecture Roadmap and the Implementation and Migration Plan come together. Above everything else, focus on the E-versus-F distinction. If you take one thing from this module into the exam, make it that.

1.title: Where E & F Sit
1.text: Let's place these phases. After Phases B, C, and D have produced a target architecture and a consolidated set of gaps, Phases E and F turn all of that into a deliverable plan. Phase E, Opportunities and Solutions, is the first round of implementation planning — it works out how we'll deliver. Phase F, Migration Planning, then finalizes the detailed, sequenced plan. Together they form the bridge between defining the architecture, in B through D, and actually implementing it, in Phase G. Keep this anchor in mind throughout: Phase E identifies the delivery vehicles, and Phase F plans and schedules them.

1.title: Phase E — Objectives
1.text: Let's start with Phase E and its objectives. First, it generates the initial, complete version of the Architecture Roadmap — the first time all the domain roadmaps come together into one. Second, it determines whether an incremental approach is needed, and if so, it identifies the Transition Architectures — those intermediate states we'll step through. And third, it identifies the delivery vehicles: the projects, programs, and portfolios that will actually deliver the target. The headline fact, which the exam tests directly: Phase E is where Transition Architectures and work packages first appear. Hold onto that.

1.title: Phase E — Key Input
1.text: What does Phase E start from? Its main input is the candidate Architecture Roadmap components produced by Phases B, C, and D — together with the consolidated gap analysis results from across those domains. Phase E takes all of that domain-by-domain material and consolidates and reconciles it into a coherent, enterprise-wide set of solutions. So Phase E doesn't start from nothing — it starts from the gaps and the candidate roadmap components that the domain phases handed it. It's a consolidation phase as much as a planning one.

1.title: Phase E — Consolidate the Gaps
1.text: The first big task in Phase E is to consolidate the gaps. You take the gap analysis results from Phases B, C, and D and integrate them into a single, unified view. The tool for this is the Consolidated Gaps, Solutions and Dependencies matrix. As its name suggests, it does three things at once: it lists the gaps, it identifies the Solution Building Blocks that could address one or more of those gaps along with their associated Architecture Building Blocks, and it captures the dependencies between them. So whenever you see a question about linking gaps to solutions and dependencies, the answer is the Consolidated Gaps, Solutions and Dependencies matrix.

1.title: Phase E — The Implementation Factor Catalog
1.text: A second Phase E technique is the Implementation Factor catalog — sometimes called the implementation factor assessment and deduction matrix. This catalog records all the factors that will influence how the architecture gets implemented: the risks, issues, assumptions, dependencies, and actions, plus the organization's change attributes. It also captures assessments of the culture, skills, and transition capability of the units involved. Think of it as the repository for your migration decisions — a record of everything that shapes the "how" of implementation. For the exam: the Implementation Factor catalog captures what will influence how the architecture is implemented.

1.title: Phase E — Work Packages
1.text: Now a key concept — the work package. A work package is a set of actions identified to achieve one or more roadmap objectives. In practical terms, it's a project, or a coherent group of changes, that delivers part of the target. In Phase E, you take all those consolidated gaps and their solutions and you group them into work packages — bundling related work together into deliverable units. Later, these work packages get assigned to actual projects for delivery. So the simple definition to remember: a work package packages the gaps and their solutions into a deliverable unit of work. We'll contrast it with Transition Architectures in a moment.

1.title: Phase E — Transition Architectures
1.text: Here's one of the most important concepts in these phases — the Transition Architecture. A Transition Architecture is a deliverable, operational, intermediate state between your baseline and your target. The key word is operational: these are incremental plateaus that the enterprise actually migrates to and runs in, reaching a consistent, working state each time. As the diagram shows, you step from the baseline, to Transition 1, to Transition 2, and onward to the target — each step a stable place to stand. You use them when the target is simply too big to reach in one leap. So distinguish this clearly from a work package: a work package is a unit of work; a Transition Architecture is an architecture state. Work packages deliver transitions.

1.title: Phase E — Capability Increments
1.text: Closely related is the idea of capability-based planning. Rather than planning purely around technology, capability-based planning focuses delivery on business outcomes — on capabilities. Within that, a capability increment is a discrete portion of a capability, delivered as one stage of building that capability up. And Transition Architectures are often aligned to these capability increments, so that each plateau the enterprise reaches corresponds to a meaningful jump in business capability. The exam connection: capability-based planning links the roadmap to business capabilities and their increments, keeping the whole delivery effort anchored to business value rather than just technical milestones.

1.title: Phase E — The Implementation & Migration Strategy
1.text: Before any detailed planning, Phase E formulates the overall Implementation and Migration Strategy. This is the big-picture approach to delivering value: deciding, for instance, whether you'll proceed incrementally through transitions or attempt a more big-bang delivery, and how you'll group the work packages. It also confirms the readiness and risk for business transformation, carrying forward the readiness assessment first done back in Phase A. The division of labour to remember is this: Phase E sets the strategy — the approach — while Phase F produces the detailed plan. Strategy in E, plan in F.

1.title: Phase E — Outputs
1.text: Let's collect Phase E's outputs. The big one is the Architecture Roadmap — this is the first time it exists as a complete, consolidated version. You also get an initial, outline version of the Implementation and Migration Plan. You get the Transition Architectures, if an incremental approach is needed. You get updates to the Capability Assessment and your set of work packages. And you update the Architecture Definition Document and the Requirements Specification. The two facts most likely to be tested: Phase E produces the first full Architecture Roadmap, and only an outline of the migration plan — the detailed plan comes next, in Phase F.

1.title: Phase F — Objectives
1.text: Now Phase F, Migration Planning. Its objectives are to finalize the Architecture Roadmap and the supporting Implementation and Migration Plan; to ensure that plan is properly coordinated with the enterprise's change-management approach and its project portfolios; and to ensure that the business value and the cost of each work package are clearly understood. Where Phase E produced an outline and a strategy, Phase F completes the detailed, agreed, and sequenced delivery plan. So if a question mentions the final, detailed, coordinated migration plan, that points to Phase F, not Phase E.

1.title: Phase F — Prioritization & Business Value
1.text: A central activity in Phase F is prioritization. You take all the projects and work packages and prioritize them by cost, value, and risk. The technique for this is the Business Value Assessment, which weighs the business value of each work package against its risk, so you can sequence the most valuable, lowest-risk work sensibly. You also confirm the Transition Architectures and the order in which you'll move through them. The exam framing: Phase F prioritizes using value versus risk, turning the candidate work from Phase E into a properly ordered roadmap. Value-versus-risk prioritization is a Phase F signature.

1.title: Phase F — The Implementation & Migration Plan
1.text: The headline output of Phase F is the detailed Implementation and Migration Plan. This is the finalized plan: the schedule, the projects, the resources, the milestones, and the dependencies, all pinned down. It aligns the work packages to the Transition Architectures and to the organization's chosen delivery vehicles. And once complete, it's handed over to the portfolio and project management functions for actual execution. Remember the lineage clearly: the outline of this plan began in Phase E, but the detailed, finalized Implementation and Migration Plan is a Phase F output. Outline in E, detail in F.

1.title: Phase F — Transition to Implementation
1.text: Phase F also handles the handover. It confirms that the architecture is genuinely ready to move into implementation governance — Phase G. It establishes the basis for the Architecture Contract that will bind the delivery teams, even though that contract is formalized in G. And it documents the lessons learned and updates the Architecture Repository with everything produced. So think of Phase F as the handover point: the moment the carefully planned architecture passes from the planning world into the world of governed delivery. Planning ends; governed execution begins.

1.title: E vs F — The Critical Distinction
1.text: This is the slide to burn into memory, because the exam tests it relentlessly. Phase E focuses on Opportunities and Solutions; Phase F focuses on Migration Planning. Phase E identifies the delivery vehicles, the work packages, and the Transition Architectures; Phase F prioritizes, sequences, and finalizes the plan. In Phase E the plan is initial and outline; in Phase F it's detailed and final. And the key question each answers differs: Phase E asks "how will we deliver?" while Phase F asks "in what order, and when?" If you can rattle off this table, you'll handle every E-versus-F question the exam throws at you. E is solutions and increments; F is the prioritized, scheduled plan.

1.title: Key Techniques Across E & F
1.text: Let's line up the key techniques and pin each to its phase, because matching technique to phase is a common question format. The Consolidated Gaps, Solutions and Dependencies matrix — that's Phase E, linking gaps to solutions and dependencies. The Implementation Factor catalog — also Phase E, capturing the factors, risks, and decisions affecting migration. The Business Value Assessment — that's Phase F, prioritizing by value versus risk. And capability-based planning spans E into F, keeping delivery outcome-focused. So: the two matrices and the factor catalog sit in E; the value-versus-risk prioritization sits in F.

1.title: How the Roadmap Evolves
1.text: Let's trace how the roadmap itself evolves, because it's a clean way to keep the phases straight. In Phases B, C, and D, each domain produces its own candidate roadmap components. In Phase E, those get consolidated into the first full Architecture Roadmap. In Phase F, that roadmap is prioritized and finalized, along with the migration plan. And in Phases G and H, it's executed, governed, and then maintained through change. So the progression is: candidate in B, C, D; consolidated in E; finalized in F. If a question asks which phase first produces a complete roadmap, the answer is E; which phase finalizes it, F.

1.title: Transition Architectures — Why They Matter
1.text: Let's reinforce why Transition Architectures matter, because the concept rewards a moment's reflection. They make a large, daunting transformation achievable in stages, with each stage delivering real, operational value rather than being a mere milestone on paper. They reduce risk, because you validate your progress at each plateau before pressing on. And they give stakeholders visible, tangible milestones to rally around. The exam-critical nuance, one more time: a Transition Architecture is not just a plan or a checkpoint — it's an architecture state that the enterprise genuinely operates in. That's what separates it from a work package or a schedule entry.

1.title: Common Exam Traps
1.text: Let's disarm the traps, and they nearly all cluster around swapping E and F. Trap one: "Phase E produces the final, detailed migration plan" — no, that's Phase F; E produces only the outline. Trap two: "Transition Architectures first appear in Phase F" — no, they first appear in Phase E. Trap three: "a work package is the same as a Transition Architecture" — no, work packages deliver transitions; they're different things, one a unit of work and one an architecture state. And trap four: "Business Value Assessment happens in Phase E" — no, that value-versus-risk prioritization is a Phase F activity. The master defence against all of these is the anchor: E identifies, F finalizes.

1.title: Key Numbers & Quick Facts (Cheat Sheet)
1.text: Here's your E-and-F cheat-sheet. Phase E is Opportunities and Solutions; Phase F is Migration Planning. The first full Architecture Roadmap comes from Phase E. The detailed Implementation and Migration Plan comes from Phase F. Transition Architectures first appear in Phase E. The gaps-to-solutions matrix is the Consolidated Gaps, Solutions and Dependencies matrix. The record of migration factors is the Implementation Factor catalog. The prioritization technique is the Business Value Assessment, in Phase F. And the overall planning style is capability-based planning. Screenshot this — it covers the recall questions for both phases.

1.title: Module Summary
1.text: Let's recap. Phases E and F convert the target architecture and its gaps into a deliverable, sequenced plan. Phase E identifies the work packages and Transition Architectures and builds the first full Architecture Roadmap. Phase F prioritizes by value versus risk and finalizes the detailed Implementation and Migration Plan. Transition Architectures are incremental, operational plateaus on the way to the target. And the one anchor that ties it all together, the one you must not forget: Phase E identifies, and Phase F finalizes. Hold that, and these two phases will never trip you up.

1.title: Bridge to Module 6
1.text: So what's next? With a finalized plan in hand, the architecture moves into execution. Phase G, Implementation Governance, governs the delivery — making sure what gets built actually matches the architecture, using a mechanism called the Architecture Contract. Phase H, Architecture Change Management, then keeps the architecture alive and relevant once it's in production. The connection to remember as we move on: the detailed plan from Phase F is exactly what Phase G governs against. That's where Module 6 picks up — the final two phases of the cycle.

1.title: Quick Self-Check
1.text: A quick self-check before the questions. From memory: can you state the one core difference between Phase E and Phase F? Can you define a Transition Architecture and say which phase introduces it? Can you name the matrix that links gaps to solutions and dependencies? And can you say which phase performs value-versus-risk prioritization? If the E-and-F distinction still feels even slightly blurry, go back and re-watch slide seventeen — that side-by-side table — before you attempt the practice questions. Clarity there is worth real marks.

1.title: One-Sentence Phase Recap (A–F so far)
1.text: Let's take stock with a one-sentence recap of everything so far. Phase A: the Vision and the Statement of Architecture Work. Phase B: the Business Architecture. Phase C: Data plus Application Architecture. Phase D: Technology Architecture. Phase E: identify the solutions, work packages, and Transition Architectures, producing the first Roadmap. And Phase F: prioritize and finalize the Implementation and Migration Plan. That's six phases down, each in a single sentence — a nice way to revise the whole front half of the ADM. Just two phases remain, G and H, and they're next.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question 1. What is the primary difference between ADM Phase E and Phase F? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. Phase E identifies delivery vehicles and Transition Architectures; Phase F prioritizes and finalizes the detailed migration plan Phase E (Opportunities & Solutions) does the first implementation planning — identifying delivery vehicles, work packages, and Transition Architectures, and producing the first full Architecture Roadmap. Phase F (Migration Planning) prioritizes by value and risk and finalizes the detailed Implementation & Migration Plan.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question 2. In which phase do Transition Architectures first appear? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is C. Phase E Transition Architectures — incremental, operational intermediate states between baseline and target — first appear in Phase E, when the architecture team determines whether an incremental approach is needed and defines the plateaus.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question 3. Which matrix consolidates the gap analysis results from Phases B–D and links them to potential solutions and dependencies? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. The Consolidated Gaps, Solutions & Dependencies matrix The Consolidated Gaps, Solutions & Dependencies matrix (created in Phase E) integrates the gaps from the Business, Information Systems, and Technology architectures and identifies SBBs that can address one or more gaps, along with their dependencies.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question 4. What best describes a Transition Architecture? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is C. A deliverable, operational intermediate state that the enterprise migrates to on the way to the target A Transition Architecture is a deliverable, operational intermediate state — an incremental "plateau" — that the enterprise actually migrates to and operates in, en route from baseline to target. It is more than a plan: it's an architecture state.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question 5. In which phase are work packages prioritized using a value-versus-risk (Business Value Assessment) approach to finalize the roadmap? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. Phase F Phase F (Migration Planning) prioritizes the work packages and projects by cost, value, and risk — using a Business Value Assessment — to produce the finalized, sequenced Architecture Roadmap and detailed Implementation & Migration Plan. Phase E sets the strategy and identifies the work; Phase F sequences it.
